source.title: Distributional Scaling Laws for Emergent Capabilities
source.authors: Rosie Zhao; Tian Qin; David Alvarez-Melis; S. Kakade; Naomi Saphra

record.file_problem: The extracted abstract begins mid-word, and some figure labels are flattened; the main text, appendices and references are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study's own results refine and challenge downstream predictability with scale: performance varies substantially across random seeds, with abrupt or nonmonotonic trends in several tasks. It does not test the original held-out cross-entropy scaling measurements or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper cites conventional scaling laws but does not fit or test held-out pretraining-loss power laws, extrapolate losses from small runs, or identify compute-optimal parameter/token splits. Rows below cover its own downstream capability results across seeds, scales or data compositions. Detailed per-scale distributions shown only in plots are summarized where the paper also describes the result in text.
record.test_reason: The study scales width and depth of toy Transformers across 200–250 seeds, and compares Qwen2.5 0.5B with 1.5B. It shows that individual-run downstream trends can be abrupt or non-monotonic, even when the mean across seeds moves smoothly. This argues V6 needs restating. It does not measure pretraining-loss power laws, extrapolation, allocation or shape effects on loss.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also explicitly contest the 'loss-to-downstream' view that scale effects are predictable and that continuous metrics smooth out breakthroughs. They argue extrapolation must model both the success probability and the performance of successful runs.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines seed-level distributions of downstream capabilities in synthetic tasks and partially reinitialized language models. It does not reproduce held-out cross-entropy scaling-law fits or compute-optimal allocation experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with random seed, model depth or width, model size, and task-data composition. The paper also reports that continuous loss metrics retain multimodal variation.

fits_no_version.finding: Raising the task-data fraction in the training mix (MMLU in C4; hierarchical sentences in question formation) shifts the probability of a successful run, with bimodal seed outcomes at intermediate ratios, including under NLL.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Task-specific data share changes success probability across seeds, producing abrupt mean jumps from gradual distribution shifts.

fits_no_version.finding: Final training loss across 80 Qwen2.5-0.5B reinitializations is unimodal and smooth, while MMLU NLL in the same setting is multimodal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Across seeds at a fixed scale, training loss does not reveal the clustered variation in downstream capability.

record.problems: The paper studies selected synthetic tasks and MMLU/question-formation settings rather than general held-out pretraining-loss scaling. The language-model experiments use reinitialized upper layers and continued pretraining on limited mixtures; most plotted distributions are not tabulated numerically. The 1.5B MMLU appendix uses 20 seeds per mixture because of computation limits.
record.rows_left_out: Not stated: no separate rows are made for every plotted scale or every MMLU mixture in Figures 18–19; the reported aggregate patterns and explicitly described conditions are retained. Figure-only numeric values are not estimated.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining-loss scaling against parameters, tokens or compute.
Width versus depth is varied, but only for downstream generalization, not for loss at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities or regimes are fitted with power laws.
No fit of downstream performance against pretraining loss. No large-scale benchmarks beyond MMLU, and only two LM sizes.

missing.what: Fraction of successful runs (>20% accuracy) and mean of successful runs both rise continuously with scale, except from depth 2 to 3.
Wasserstein-L2 distance to the largest scale drops sharply at depth 3 or width 2 heads, marking abrupt onset of bimodality before the mode breakthrough.
Depth-1 models fail to length-generalize at any width despite near-perfect in-distribution accuracy.
Fixed seeds can give highly emergent or highly linear scaling curves under identical training (breakthroughness and linearity metrics).
Count-task depth scaling trends resemble addition: mode, mean and success fraction improve with depth.

record.verdict_notes: Most evidence comes from toy Transformers trained from scratch on synthetic tasks, and from partially reinitialized Qwen models, so bearing on V6 for large-scale pretraining is indirect. Rows that vary data-mixture ratio rather than scale, and rows giving single-setting seed distributions, were unlinked from V6 and moved to fits_no_version. Most values come from figures, and numeric distributions are not tabulated.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining-loss scaling against parameters, tokens or compute is measured.
No small-run loss fit is used to predict larger-run loss.
No fixed-compute parameter/token allocation is tested.
No loss comparison at fixed parameter count across architecture shapes is reported.
The study does not test power-law scaling across other modalities or the listed training regimes.

Tests selected synthetic length-generalization, MMLU and question-formation results, including seed variability and some scale or data changes; it does not test general downstream predictability across benchmarks or fit downstream performance against pretraining loss.
It does not compare fitted power-law exponents, parameter-counting choices, or compute-optimal splits across fitting setups.

rows.value: Distributions cluster into high- and low-performance modes at many parameter sizes; different seeds show emergent or smoother trends.

rows.check: Bimodal accuracy across seeds means single runs can be emergent or smooth. Predictability holds only distributionally.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-0.5B and Qwen2.5-1.5B
rows.stage_stated: continued pretraining after reinitializing the final attention layer and LM head
rows.operation_detail: Compared model sizes after continued pretraining on the same C4 and MMLU mixture

conditions.value: 0.5B for 2 epochs; 1.5B for 5 epochs; learning rate 1e-5 with linear decay

relationships.condition: Toy Transformers on reverse-order addition, scaling width or depth, 200 seeds per scale
relationships.reason: The mean rises smoothly with scale (R4), but seed distributions are bimodal and the mode jumps (R1–R3, R5). Predictability holds only for the seed distribution, not for single runs.
relationships.display_finding: Mean accuracy increased smoothly, but bimodal seed distributions and shifting modes made individual runs unpredictable.

tranche.reason: The study explicitly contests deterministic downstream predictability and reports seed-dependent breakthroughs and inverse scaling, requiring V6 to be qualified.

source_check.notes: The supplied text is v5, dated February 2026, titled Random Scaling of Emergent Capabilities; the pack lists a different title and 2025. The study characterizes distributions but does not validate forecasts of full seed distributions at larger scales.

statements.correction: V6 label=limits_scope for the cited addition and question-formation results; addition mean improves more continuously than its mode; continuous metrics remain bimodal; at 90% hierarchical data, most 6-layer question-formation seeds achieve 100% OOD accuracy and some achieve 0%.
statements.problem: The description of this study is accurate, but its challenges label overstates these cited results: they qualify individual-run predictability without establishing an aggregate reversal.
